title: The Lord looks on the heart (1 Samuel 16:1–13)
hookLine: the youngest son, out with the sheep, is chosen and anointed

lines: HOW LONG WILT THOU MOURN FOR SAUL?
cards: An old prophet is grieving, and God tells him to stop: "How long wilt thou mourn for Saul, seeing I have rejected him from reigning over Israel? fill thine horn with oil, and go."

The tall king from yesterday has gone wrong, and Samuel can't let go of him. He's sent to Bethlehem, to Jesse, grandson of Ruth and Boaz. Samuel is afraid: "How can I go? if Saul hear it, he will kill me."
So he goes quietly, with a heifer for a sacrifice, and invites Jesse and his sons. One of them is about to be anointed king. Samuel doesn't know which.

teach.h: SURELY THE LORD'S ANOINTED IS BEFORE HIM.
teach.b: Jesse's son Eliab walks in first, and Samuel thinks he's found him: "Surely the LORD'S anointed is before him."

teach.h: THE LORD LOOKETH ON THE HEART.
teach.b: God answers with the line that names today: "Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart."
Yesterday the crowd cheered a king taller than everyone from the shoulders up. Samuel is about to be drawn by height again, and God stops him.
The sons pass by: "Jesse made seven of his sons to pass before Samuel. And Samuel said unto Jesse, The LORD hath not chosen these." Then: "Are here all thy children?"
Jesse admits, "There remaineth yet the youngest, and, behold, he keepeth the sheep." Nobody thought to call him in. Samuel says, we will not sit down till he comes.
Until now, the story hasn't said his name. He arrives, and the text, with a little smile, describes him anyway: "ruddy, and withal of a beautiful countenance, and goodly to look to."
The point was never that looks are bad. It's that they aren't what God goes by. "Arise, anoint him: for this is he."

teach.h: ONLY THEN DOES THE NAME APPEAR.
teach.b: Samuel pours the oil in front of his brothers, and only then does the name appear: "the Spirit of the LORD came upon David from that day forward." Samuel goes home to Ramah. Nothing in these verses makes the boy king yet.

how: Christians read 1 Samuel 16:7 as a reminder that God does not judge by appearance, and read the anointing of the youngest son alongside other stories in scripture where God chooses the overlooked.

o: the prophet who poured oil on David's head
the youngest son, who kept his father's sheep
the son Samuel almost anointed for his looks

games.q: in Jesse's house — tap the pairs.
p: filled with oil for the anointing

s: Samuel recognized David as the chosen one right away
he thought it was Eliab, until God told him to look not on his countenance (16:6–7).
the text describes David as plain to look at
ruddy, of a beautiful countenance, and goodly to look to (16:12). looks just weren't how God chose.
Jesse didn't bring his youngest son to the sacrifice
he was keeping the sheep, and Samuel had to ask, are here all thy children? (16:11).

games.q: you're Samuel. seven of Jesse's sons have passed by you, and God has said no to each. what do you do?
o: choose the best of the seven anyway.
ask, are here all thy children?
go home and tell God there's no one.
games.why: Jesse admits there's one more, the youngest, out with the sheep. Samuel won't sit down till he comes (16:11).

practice: Think of one person you've sized up by the outside, their clothes, age, accent, job, the way they talk: someone you'd have left out with the sheep.
Hold their face for a moment and try to look past it: what do you actually know of their heart? If you pray, ask to see them the way the text says God sees.
